summary: TURN 2 ON THIS BEAD. Turn 1 built the whole mechanism and parked it in plant/tools/ because the ticket's gate names scripts/loop-brief.selftest.mjs and loop-work.yml's containment regex is ^(\.github/loop/(outbox|work)/|plant/). That is still true and I did not re-litigate it. What I found instead is that TURN 1'S ENTIRE OUTBOX WAS STILL SITTING ON DISK, UNAPPLIED: loop-work applies an outbox only when ticketgate != failed, and this bead's gate names a file no seat can create, so it fails whatever the turn does. Turn 1's dead-end, its decision and its finding never reached the ledger, the bead stayed 'ready', and it was re-dispatched to me. I would have DESTROYED that record by writing this file, since the outbox path is the same. It is carried forward below, marked, so it survives whichever turn is finally applied. Then I did real work rather than re-parking: I read turn 1's output and fixed TWO defects in it, both of which it had the information to see and one of which it explicitly named and declined. (1) THE CLIP TOOK THE HEAD ONLY. Turn 1's own finding says the findings in this ledger narrate a discovery and put what transfers at the END ('THE GENERAL LESSON, which is the part that transfers'), so a 1600-char head-clip keeps the anecdote and drops the lesson — the precise inversion of what a turn needs. clip() now keeps a head AND a tail with the elision marked between them, CLIP_HEAD_FRACTION 0.56, degrading to the old head-clip below MIN_MIDDLE_CLIP_CHARS=400. head+tail is EXACTLY the old allowance, so every byte-budget number in the gate is unchanged by construction. (2) AN EMPTY TICKET SELECTED ZERO FINDINGS. ticketTerms({}) is empty, so every finding scores 0 and MIN_SCORE drops all of them — and {} is exactly what the PLAN and REVIEW seats pass, the plan seat being the one whose whole job is writing requirements out of what the loop has learned. It would have been handed an empty findings section with nothing red anywhere: this repo's most-repeated failure (a channel that cannot carry the thing, failing silently) reproduced inside the mechanism meant to improve the channel. selectMemory now distinguishes 'measured and found irrelevant' (score 0 -> drop) from 'nothing to measure against' (no terms -> fall back to the RECENCY_FALLBACK=12 most recent), and the footer says which of the two rules ran. GATE SECTIONS ADDED, each with the control that makes it bite: §10 asserts the moral survives the clip AND asserts the moral lies BEYOND the allowance in the source, so a head-clip provably could not have kept it — without that control the section passes for the rule it replaced; it also asserts the kept head and kept tail are NOT ADJACENT in the source, which is false for any contiguous window (I replaced a first draft that asserted !clipped.includes(NARRATION), which cannot fail since 4000 chars never fit 1600 — decoration wearing a control's label). §11 is a PAIR OF RUNS over one ledger differing in one thing: with a ticket the OLDEST finding is kept and the NEWEST dropped; without one they swap exactly. Neither run alone distinguishes 'ranked by score' from 'ranked by age'. Its second control is a ticket that HAS terms and matches nothing, which must still select nothing — the fallback must never quietly undo MIN_SCORE. HONESTLY, AND IT IS THE SAME CAVEAT TURN 1 GAVE: no Bash, so I ran none of it. I hand-traced the whole file — every ticket term, every fixture score (noise 9, star 30, weak 1, unrelated 0, dead-ends 0), the sort tie-break that makes the fallback branch correct without a second sort, and the composed size at roughly 85KB against 131072. The one number I am least sure of is §6's 20%-headroom assertion, which rests on my arithmetic about newline-indentation overhead; if this file goes red that is where I would look first. I deliberately did NOT move it into plant/test/, upholding turn 1's decision for turn 1's reason: that glob gates every creates-gate turn and every deploy-plant publish, and an unrun self-written test about brief composition could halt the fleet with nobody watching.

learned.title: A blocked turn's outbox is committed and NEVER APPLIED — and the next turn on the bead overwrites it at the same path
learned.body:
Found by opening .github/loop/outbox/lp-14c7f5.json before writing to it, and discovering a complete turn's record already there.

THE MECHANISM. loop-work.yml applies the outbox only when the outbox is valid AND ticketgate != failed. This bead's gate is `node scripts/loop-brief.selftest.mjs`, a file no agent seat can create (containment is `^(\.github/loop/(outbox|work)/|plant/)`), so ticketgate is FAILED whatever the turn does. Turn 1 therefore produced a dead-end, a decision, a finding, two well-formed proposals and an ask, all of them correct, and NONE of it reached the ledger. The bead stayed `ready` and was re-dispatched to me.

THE PART THAT MAKES IT A DEAD-END RATHER THAN A BUG REPORT: the outbox filename is derived from the BEAD, not from the turn. `.github/loop/outbox/<bead>.json`. So the second turn on any bead writes to the same path as the first, and the staging step commits it. A turn that does the obvious correct thing — write its outbox as instructed — SILENTLY DESTROYS the unapplied record of every previous attempt on that bead. Nothing warns it. The instruction it is given says 'write EXACTLY ONE file' at that path.

The two halves compound into a ratchet: a bead that cannot pass its gate can never close, so it is re-dispatched forever, and each dispatch erases the previous one's diagnosis. Turn 3 would have found a pristine-looking tree, no record of turns 1 or 2, and rediscovered the same thing a third time. The memory this very ticket exists to improve cannot record the reason it is failing.

WHAT I DID ABOUT IT: carried turn 1's learnings and proposals into this outbox verbatim, marked as carried. That is a manual fix that only works because I looked. It does not scale and the next turn may not think to look.

THE FIX, and it is small: apply the `learned` array even when ticketgate fails, while still refusing to mark the bead done. A failed or blocked turn's findings are the most valuable thing it produces — they are precisely what stops turn 30 repeating turn 4, which is the stated purpose of the ledger. Alternatively, or additionally, name the outbox `<bead>-<turn>.json` so a second attempt cannot overwrite the first. The first fix is better because it puts the record where it is read; the second is a cheap backstop that needs no policy decision.

GENERAL SHAPE, and it is this repo's most-recorded one aimed at a new target: every previous instance was a channel that could not carry a message. This is a channel that carries the message and then a later, correct action overwrites it. Append-only was chosen for the ledger for exactly this reason; the outbox is the one artefact in the chain that is last-write-wins, and it is the one holding the diagnoses of turns that failed.

learned.title: The brief selector handed the PLANNER an empty findings section — the seat whose entire job is turning findings into requirements
learned.body:
loop-brief.mjs scores a finding by lexical overlap with the ticket and drops anything scoring below MIN_SCORE=1. That rule is right and it is what makes the mechanism SELECTION rather than truncation.

The plan and review seats have NO TICKET. The module's own wiring note says to pass a synthetic one 'or `{}`'. Feed it `{}`: ticketTerms returns an empty Map, every finding scores 0, MIN_SCORE drops all of them, and the seat gets dead-ends and nothing else. Turn 1 wrote that outcome down as 'a defensible floor rather than a crash' and it is neither — it is a total loss of the accumulated findings for the one seat that exists to write requirements out of them, with nothing red anywhere.

THE DISTINCTION THE CODE WAS MISSING, and it is the whole fix:

    a score of zero   =  measured, and found irrelevant   -> drop it
    NO TICKET AT ALL  =  there was nothing to measure     -> cannot drop it

These are different facts and the second was being rendered as the first. Fixed: when the ticket yields no terms at all, selection falls back to the RECENCY_FALLBACK=12 most recent findings, and the footer says which of the two rules ran so a turn can tell whether it was given the relevant ones or merely the recent ones.

Note what recency is doing here and what it is not. The ticket that commissioned this mechanism says plainly that truncating by age is wrong, and it IS wrong — WHEN A BETTER RULE IS AVAILABLE. With no ticket there is no better rule, and 'the most recent 12' beats 'none'. The fallback is explicitly forbidden from firing on a ticket that has terms and matches nothing, because that would quietly undo MIN_SCORE; the gate has a control for exactly that.

THE TRANSFERABLE PART: a scoring function's degenerate input is not automatically its correct default. 'Everything scored 0' can mean two opposite things and the code had no way to tell them apart, so it picked the destructive reading. Any threshold applied to a computed score should ask first whether the score was computable at all. This is the fourth entry in this ledger of the same shape — a scalar summary standing in for a structure (verdictLine reading deficits[0]; `bound` naming one starved input of several; level.mjs's network.ok going vacuously true) — and it is the first where the collapsed information was 'was this measured'.

learned.title: Clip the MIDDLE of a finding, not its tail — turn 1 named this fix, priced it as a second behaviour, and declined it; I took it
learned.body:
Turn 1's finding says it exactly: 'the load-bearing sentence of a long one is often at the END, after the narration of how it was discovered'. It is right, and the ledger proves it on itself — findings here close with 'THE GENERAL LESSON, which is the part that transfers', 'the transferable rule', 'the generalisable bit', 'the general shape, and it is the same one this ledger keeps recording'. A head-clip at 1600 characters keeps the anecdote and discards the lesson.

Turn 1 declined the fix on two grounds: it is a second behaviour to test, and a middle-clip is 'a guess about document structure that I have evidence for but have not measured'. I took it anyway, and the reasoning is the part worth recording.

The second ground overstates the risk because THE TOTAL KEPT IS IDENTICAL. head + tail === maxChars exactly, so this changes WHICH characters survive and not HOW MANY — every byte-budget number in the gate is unaffected by construction rather than by re-measurement. The cost of being wrong is therefore bounded to legibility, and legibility is what is being traded FOR: a fragment ending mid-narration versus a fragment that also carries the conclusion.

The first ground is real and I paid it: §10 exists, with the control that makes it bite (the moral is asserted to lie beyond the allowance in the SOURCE, so a head-clip provably could not have kept it).

CONSTANTS AND WHAT WOULD REVERSE THEM. CLIP_HEAD_FRACTION 0.56 gives 896/704 on a finding and 1792/1408 on a dead-end — turn 1's own suggested '~900 and ~700', which I adopted rather than invented. MIN_MIDDLE_CLIP_CHARS 400: below that, two fragments of ~200 characters are less legible than one continuous one and there is no room for a narration-then-moral shape to exist, so it degrades to the old head-clip. Both are plain character slices, not sentence- or line-aware: a structural cut is a guess that can be wrong invisibly, a character offset is a thing a reader can verify by counting.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: anyone reading a composed brief and finding the seams harder to read than a clean head-clip. That is a taste judgement, it is exactly the kind no gate can make, and it is one edit to CLIP_HEAD_FRACTION = 1.0 to undo — which is why I was willing to make the call unattended.

learned.title: [CARRIED FROM TURN 1, NEVER APPLIED] The loop dispatched a ticket its own containment gate makes IMPOSSIBLE — and the destructive branch would have erased the evidence
learned.body:
lp-14c7f5 names `scripts/loop-brief.selftest.mjs` as the gate it creates. loop-work.yml's containment gate is a hardcoded regex, ^(\.github/loop/(outbox|work)/|plant/), and scripts/ is not in it. So the ticket is unsatisfiable by the seat it was dispatched to, and no amount of skill inside the turn changes that.

WHAT MAKES IT A DEAD-END RATHER THAN A BUG REPORT is the failure shape. The gate does not reject the offending file, it runs `git checkout -- . && git clean -fd` over the whole tree. `clean -fd` removes untracked files, and the outbox is an untracked file. So an agent that does the obvious, correct-looking thing — write the deliverable where the ticket says — loses the deliverable AND the outbox AND every finding it wrote, and the run reports gate=failed with no record of what was attempted. The next turn on the bead has no way to learn any of this and does the same thing.

SECOND-ORDER, AND WORSE: loop-work applies the outbox to the ledger only `if outbox.valid && ticketgate != failed`. This ticket's gate is a command naming a file no seat can create, so ticketgate is failed WHATEVER the turn does. A blocked turn's learnings therefore never reach the ledger. [TURN 2 CONFIRMS THIS EMPIRICALLY: turn 1's outbox was still on disk, unapplied, when turn 2 opened it. See turn 2's dead-end on the overwrite hazard.]

THIS IS THE SIXTH INSTANCE OF ONE PATTERN. The ledger already records five: the brief taught creates-gate and the outbox schema had no field; the reviewer could not wake the tick on a zero-promote; the worker's propose schema omitted class/gate; the planner could not wake the tick at all; every seat's push loop could not survive a conflict in a generated file. Each time a component was right and the CHANNEL between it and the next stage could not carry the result. This one is the same shape aimed at the WORK ITSELF: the ticket factory can express a requirement the executor is structurally forbidden to satisfy, and nothing between them compares the two.

THE CHEAP CHECK, and it belongs at dispatch: loop-tick already knows the bead and can read config.json. Before issuing a work order, assert that every path a bead's `gate` names falls inside the containment regex. A bead whose gate lives outside the fleet's write scope is not dispatchable — fail closed, exactly as the class taxonomy does for an untagged bead.

AND THE DEEPER ONE: the containment regex and config.writes are TWO LISTS OF THE SAME THING, already drifted (writes has loop/**, containment does not). This repo has already paid for exactly this — loop-work's staging step used to be a hardcoded list that did not include plant/ and silently discarded the first live turn's entire output. The containment set is the third copy and it was not brought along.

learned.title: [CARRIED FROM TURN 1, NEVER APPLIED — and upheld by turn 2] Parked in plant/tools/ rather than plant/test/: verification traded for a blast radius neither turn could bound
learned.body:
Both are inside containment, so both survive. The difference is that everything matching plant/test/*.selftest.mjs is executed by loop-work's whole-suite check on EVERY creates-gate turn, and by deploy-plant before it publishes. Putting the selftest there would have had it RUN in this very workflow run, and with no Bash that execution is the only real verification available — a genuinely large prize, and the ledger has roughly twenty findings complaining about exactly its absence.

Turn 1 chose against it: the suite is plant's, and this file is loop infrastructure with nothing to do with the game. If the unrun, self-written test is wrong it does not fail alone — it fails the gate of every future creates-gate turn and blocks every plant deploy, and stop.repeatedGateFailures is 3, so a bug in a file about brief composition could halt the fleet, unattended, for a reason no later turn would connect to this one. A bounded loss (unverified work, the loop's normal condition) against an unbounded one (the loop stops and nobody is there).

TURN 2 UPHELD IT, and had a reason turn 1 did not: turn 2 changed two behaviours in the file. The odds that an unrun file is correct go down with every edit, and the assertion turn 2 is least sure of (§6's headroom check, which rests on hand arithmetic about newline-indentation overhead) is precisely the kind that fails for reasons unrelated to the code under test. Promoting it into the fleet-wide suite on that basis would have been trading a bounded loss for an unbounded one at a WORSE moment, not a better one.

WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT: a human, or any turn with Bash, running `node plant/tools/loop-brief.selftest.mjs` once. If it passes, moving it to scripts/ (its home) makes the question moot, because scripts/ selftests are not in plant's glob either. The trade only exists while the file is parked.

Second, smaller decision, still true after turn 2: the module imports NOTHING — not even scripts/lib/beads.mjs, whose bead shape it operates on — and touches no filesystem, purely so the pair is location-independent and the move home is two `git mv` with zero edits.

learned.title: [CARRIED FROM TURN 1, NEVER APPLIED — half of it is now fixed] N=24 and the clip lengths are the two numbers no gate can justify, and only one of them was safe
learned.body:
Turn 1's original finding, carried because it never reached the ledger, with turn 2's disposition appended.

The selection rule is testable end to end and the gate tests it. What the gate CANNOT say is whether 24 findings is the right number, or whether clipping a finding to 1600 characters keeps the part that mattered.

THE CAP IS THE SAFE ONE. It is a pure resource dial: too low and a turn is under-informed, too high and the brief creeps back toward the problem this ticket exists to fix, and either way the failure is gradual and reversible by editing one constant. Nothing depends on 24 being correct. STILL TRUE, STILL UNJUSTIFIED, and still fine.

THE CLIP WAS NOT SAFE. The findings in this ledger are not uniformly dense: the load-bearing sentence of a long one is often at the END, after the narration of how it was discovered. A head-clip at 1600 characters takes the story and drops the moral, which is the precise inversion of what you would want. Turn 1 chose head-clipping anyway because it is the only rule that needs no model call and cannot be wrong in a way that hides itself, and named the cheap improvement: 'clip the MIDDLE, keeping the first ~900 and last ~700 characters with the elision marked between them'.

TURN 2 DID THAT. clip() is now a middle-clip at those exact proportions, with §10 of the gate pinning it and a control asserting a head-clip provably could not have passed. So this finding is half-closed: the clip question is answered, the cap question is not, and the cap question does not need answering.

WHAT REMAINS UNMEASURED, and it is worth stating so nobody thinks the middle-clip settled it: nobody has read a composed brief and judged whether 1600 characters of a finding, split 896/704, is enough to act on. That is a taste judgement about a document, it needs a person, and it is cheap to get once anyone is looking at a real brief.

propose.title: [CARRIED FROM TURN 1] Derive loop-work's containment gate from config.writes — the third copy of one list, and it has already drifted
propose.body:
loop-work.yml's containment ALLOWED regex is hardcoded as ^(\.github/loop/(outbox|work)/|plant/). .github/loop/config.json's `writes` says loop/**, .github/loop/**, plant/**. These are two statements of the same fact and they already disagree. The staging step three hundred lines below derives from `writes` precisely because a hardcoded copy of it silently discarded the first live turn's entire output, and the comment there says the write set and the stage set must come from one source or they drift invisibly. The containment set is the third copy and was not brought along.

WHY IT IS WORTH DOING BEYOND TIDINESS: it makes the fleet's write scope a single reviewable line in a JSON file rather than a regex buried in a workflow, which is the precondition for ever answering 'may the loop edit its own machinery' as a deliberate decision instead of by accident. Today the answer is 'no, in one place, and yes, in another'.

SCOPE, and this is the honest part: whoever takes this must decide whether widening containment to match `writes` (which adds loop/**) is intended, or whether `writes` should narrow to match containment. Turn 1 believed the first — loop/ is the monitoring surface and its data file is generated by the same commit anyway — but that is a judgement about blast radius and it is the reviewer's.

THE GATE IT CREATES: scripts/loop-containment.selftest.mjs, asserting that the regex built from a given `writes` list (a) matches every path in that list's directories, (b) rejects foam/, scripts/, .github/workflows/ and docs/ when they are absent from it, (c) is anchored, so a path merely CONTAINING an allowed prefix is refused, and (d) matches the regex literal currently in loop-work.yml when fed the current config, so the change is provably a refactor before it is a widening.

PRECONDITION, STATED PLAINLY: this touches .github/workflows/ and scripts/, both OUTSIDE the containment gate it is about. No agent seat can execute it — the change is its own blocker. It needs an operator, or it needs to be sequenced after the write scope is widened. Do not dispatch it to the fleet expecting it to land; it will produce exactly the outcome lp-14c7f5 produced twice.

propose.title: [CARRIED FROM TURN 1, and turn 2 confirmed its second half empirically] Refuse to dispatch a bead whose gate names a file outside the fleet's write scope, and keep a failed turn's findings
propose.body:
lp-14c7f5 was dispatched with the gate `node scripts/loop-brief.selftest.mjs`. No agent seat can create a file in scripts/. The turn was unsatisfiable before it started, and it has now cost TWO full turns of model budget to discover that from the inside — the second one only because the first one's diagnosis was thrown away.

loop-tick already has everything needed to catch it: it reads the bead (it filters on class and tags) and it reads config.json (it reads the budget block). The check is: for each command in the bead's `gate`, take every token ending in a source extension — the same conservative token rule `beads promote` already uses for its existence check — and assert the path falls inside the containment scope. If it does not, the bead is NOT DISPATCHABLE. Fail closed, exactly as an untagged bead is treated as not-class-A: the cost of being wrong is a bead that sits still, which is visible and cheap; the cost of the current behaviour is an unbounded series of wasted turns reporting gate=failed for a reason nobody can act on.

WHY THE REACTOR AND NOT PROMOTION: promotion is a good place for it too and already has a filesystem. But promotion happened for this bead when the operator wrote it, and the scope can change afterwards. The reactor is the last point before spend, and the ledger's hardest-won budget lesson is that the meter belongs at the point of spend rather than at a downstream component that may never run.

SECOND HALF, AND TURN 2 VERIFIED IT ON DISK RATHER THAN BY READING THE YAML: a blocked turn's outbox is committed to the branch and NEVER APPLIED, because loop-work applies it only if ticketgate != failed. Turn 1's outbox for this bead was still sitting in .github/loop/outbox/ when turn 2 opened it — one complete turn's dead-end, decision, finding, two proposals and an ask, none of it in the ledger, and turn 2 was instructed to write to that same path, which would have destroyed it. Apply the `learned` array on a gate failure while still refusing to mark the bead done; and/or name the outbox <bead>-<turn>.json so a second attempt cannot overwrite the first. A failed turn's findings are the most valuable thing it produces.

THE GATE — and note it is NOT a new one: scripts/loop-tick.selftest.mjs already exists and passes, so this is class-a proper (certified against an existing gate) with assertions added to it — assert that a fixture bead gated on scripts/x.mjs is not dispatchable under a config whose writes are plant/**, that the same bead IS dispatchable once scripts/** is added, that a gate naming no path at all (e.g. `test -f plant/index.html`) is unaffected, and that a grep pattern containing a slash is not mistaken for a path.

PRECONDITION: touches scripts/ and is therefore outside the fleet's write scope today, same as its sibling above. Operator work until that changes.

asks.title: [CARRIED FROM TURN 1, NEVER APPLIED] May the loop write its own machinery? Two turns have now been spent proving it cannot, and the answer is a risk judgement no gate can make
asks.body: Every agent seat is confined to plant/ plus its outbox. That boundary is what keeps a turn off the public web and out of the workflows that spend money, and it is stated as a security property rather than a convenience. It is also the thing that makes a whole class of ticket unsatisfiable: lp-14c7f5 asks for a file in scripts/, the reactor happily dispatched it TWICE, and no possible turn could have delivered it. The proposals both turns produced about the loop's own plumbing are all in the same position — they are their own blockers. This is not decidable from inside a turn because it is not a question about correctness (the mechanism is easy to build either way), it is a question about how much of its own machinery you are willing to let an unattended fleet edit while you are asleep, and only you can price that.
asks.do: Run `node plant/tools/loop-brief.selftest.mjs` — the deliverable two turns have now parked, and the one thing neither could do. Then open .github/workflows/loop-work.yml at the containment gate (the ALLOWED regex, ~line 314) and .github/loop/config.json's `writes` array and read them side by side.
asks.watch: Whether the selftest passes at all — no turn has ever executed it. Then, specifically, whether the loop editing the code that composes its own prompt feels different in kind from the loop editing plant/. I think it does and I could not tell you where the line is: a turn that changes what turns are told is the one edit whose mistakes are invisible to every gate downstream, because everything downstream reads the output of the thing that broke.
asks.soThat: If NO, both proposals are permanently operator work and should be tagged human-only rather than sitting in the queue looking dispatchable — and the reactor fix becomes the important one, because it stops the loop wasting turns on tickets it cannot reach. If YES BUT NARROWLY — say scripts/loop-*.mjs and nothing else — the containment regex should come from config.writes and you add that one glob, and this ticket finishes itself on the next dispatch. If YES BROADLY, the write scope, the staging list and the containment regex should collapse into one list today, before a fourth copy appears.
